title: The Rocker
full_review:
"There are no second acts in American lives." So wrote Jazz Age novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald (1896-1940). "The Rocker" (Fox Atomic), a sporadically funny comedy starring Rainn Wilson -- probably best known for his role on the NBC series "The Office" -- tells a different story.

Wilson is Robert "Fish" Fishman, a veteran drummer who, 20 years ago, was cruelly dumped by his band mates in the big-haired, head-banging group Vesuvius, just before they catapulted to fame. Embittered and unmotivated, he works at a dead-end insurance job and winds up having to move in with his sister (Jane Lynch), brother-in-law (Jeff Garlin) and nephew Matt (Josh Gad).

Despite being somewhat socially challenged, Matt belongs to a band himself, called ADD. Led by angst-ridden singer-songwriter Curtis (Teddy Geiger), ADD also features too-cool-to-smile guitarist Amelia (Emma Stone). However, just as the young musicians are about to enjoy their moment in the sun playing at their school prom, their drummer is grounded, and in desperation they turn to Fish.

Their musical styles are worlds apart, and Fish ends up ruining a slow-dance number with his outlandish antics. But the four are soon on their way to fame thanks to Fish's fondness for practicing in the nude, and his mistaking a computer camera for a microphone. When his stylings au naturel are uploaded to YouTube and word of mouth spreads about "the naked drummer," the music industry comes calling in the person of smarmy manager David (Jason Sudeikis).

As the quartet takes to the road, Fish's paternal bond with Curtis -- whose depressive lyrics are inspired by his real father's early desertion -- is strained by his budding romantic interest in Curtis' mother, Kim (Christina Applegate), who's come along as chaperone.

Director Peter Cattaneo's portrait of a likable lunkhead touches on themes of maturity and reconciliation. In keeping with the rock 'n' roll milieu, its values are somewhat hedonistic, but this is largely a matter of talk, since Mom is there to supervise, and even the seemingly irresponsible Fish will not allow any underage drinking.

The film contains brief rear nudity, nonmarital cohabitation, sexual and scatological humor, one use of the f-word and some crass language, and drug and venereal disease references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
